Doc M3 mood is 'earned trust — the way I work with agents is something my staff engineer and my CISO can sign off on, before I even try anything big,' and M3-detail opens 'Veto-stakeholder module... discipline is installed before M4's first unwatched send-off, so nobody feels exposed when the long run finally happens.' The Big Idea's reframe of trust away from surveillance ('watching harder') toward runnable verification is exactly the mechanism the doc's sign-off framing depends on. No drift.

One-sentence state: student leaves this piece having earned two sign-offs (staff engineer on the test-strategy skill, CISO on the STRIDE/ADR decision) rather than having survived a compliance check, and that earned-not-surveilled trust is what lets M4 send a session off unwatched without anyone (including the student) feeling exposed. L109 'Next': 'Two signatures, earned... Module 4 turns the discipline inward.' matches doc mood 'earned trust' and bridges directly into the doc's stated M3→M4 sequencing ('discipline installed before M4's first unwatched send-off'). Mood is honoured, not flattened or resolved early — M4 still owns the actual send-off experience.

rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Lead with discipline, not failure mode.
rules_evaluated.evidence: Big Idea leads with 'verification,' not a failure word. Section headers (Earn the trust / Sharpen the skill from evidence / Read the sharpen with a skeptical eye / Clear the session / Key Concepts / Optional challenges / Bring to Module 4 / Next) are all discipline- or action-named, none failure-named. 'STRIDE' (L39) and 'the lethal trifecta' (L16) are failure-shaped names but both are named canonical results (Kohnfelder & Garg 1999 memo; Willison's trifecta) — the rule's own carve-out example names the lethal trifecta explicitly, so both stay as-is.

Two doc-contradicted design claims, both confirmed against the actual sibling exercise files (not just the doc): (1) L23 WYL bullet claims access-control-analysis AND STRIDE each run 'as a subagent, fresh context.' Doc M3-detail: 'Subagents introduced, deliberately — and only once. The STRIDE pass is the dispatch... The access-surface pass invokes its skill in-thread... That three-way contrast is half the pedagogy.' Confirmed current: curriculum/exercises/map-the-access-surface.md L106 (commit 4589f1d5, 2026-09-04, after this file's pin 85515fa0): 'This exercise invokes its skill in-thread, and that is the design... Do not add a dispatch clause here to match the module's subagent theme.' (2) L26 WYL bullet ('invoke it on the security-tested feature') plus maintainer L152 and L196 ('run the skill on the feature you just security-tested') all contradict the doc: 'Invocation closes the loop, and it runs on the whole codebase in the quality-side worktree rather than on the security-tested feature: the skill is a claim about how testing works here, so the honest test of it is the repo, not one feature.' Confirmed against the actual exercise: curriculum/exercises/author-test-strategy-skill.md Phase 2 header 'Invoke the skill on this codebase' / body 'Ask Claude to invoke the skill on this codebase and grade what it produced.' Harm this rule guards against — a cross-exercise design bet (which thread does which job; feature-scope vs. codebase-scope) getting misstated in the surface a trainer reads to coach the room — is present, not hypothetical: L152/L196 sit in the maintainer's own Push-back-moves and Decision-points tables, i.e. the trainer script, and would coach students toward the wrong invocation target on both counts.
rules_evaluated.fix_hint: L23: scope 'each as a subagent' to STRIDE only — access-control-analysis runs in-thread per map-the-access-surface.md L106. L26, L152, L196: replace 'invoke...on the security-tested feature' with 'invoke...on this codebase' (the quality-side worktree), matching author-test-strategy-skill.md Phase 2 and the doc's own stated reasoning.
